Outbound C2 to PCPJack Sliver server 213.136.80.73 (esp. port 9000) AICommand & Control Medium
Detect any host beaconing to the PCPJack Sliver C2 IP 213.136.80.73 — particularly the port 9000 health-check the diagnostic script polls and the SCP/SSH (22) and HTTPS callbacks beacons use. Highest-confidence indicator in the article: the C2 IP itself was confirmed open and live by Hunt.io. Rationale: 213.136.80.73 is the unauthenticated PCPJack C2 server Hunt.io confirmed live with ports 8444/9443/9000 exposed; pivoting on the IP alone is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Hunt.io's write-up and the prior SentinelOne PCPJack analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/cloud-worm-evicts-teampcp-and-steals-credentials-at-scale/

Step 1 — Triage: identify host, process and user; pull process tree (Sliver implant typically dropped at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux) and check for Chisel binaries on disk. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via EDR, block 213.136.80.73 and 38.242.204.245 egress at perimeter, snapshot for forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound traffic for SOCKS5 listener ports 10000-14999, SCP to 38.242.204.245, SMTP probes to smtp.gmail.com:587, and persistence (cron/systemd) referencing /var/tmp/.xs.

PCPJack SMTP quality-gate probe to smtp.gmail.com:587 from non-mail Linux workloads AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunt for the Sliver deployer's outbound 'mail relay capability' probe to smtp.gmail.com:587, which the script uses to filter beacons worth keeping. A cloud VM (AWS/GCP/Azure) opening port 587 to gmail from a non-mail workload is a sharp PCPJack-specific signal. Rationale: The article's SMTP quality gate is literally a TCP 587 probe to smtp.gmail.com — extremely specific behaviour for a non-mail workload. Confirmed by Hunt.io's primary source. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1090 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate mail relay or transactional-mail VM (Postfix/Sendmail) actually configured to send via Gmail
  • Application-tier code using Gmail SMTP for password-reset or notification email
  • DevOps test of newly-built golden image's outbound mail capability
  • Backup/monitoring agent sending alert email via personal Gmail
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["mailrelay01","mailrelay02","smtp-egress-01"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (dynamic(["postfix","sendmail","opendkim","msmtp","exim4"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm whether the source host is a sanctioned mail relay (check IPAM/CMDB). If not, capture full process tree — the initiating process should be the Sliver implant at /var/tmp/.xs or a Chisel binary. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, block egress to 213.136.80.73 and 38.242.204.245, suspend cloud instance credentials. Step 3 — Hunt: search same host for the deployer script artefacts (cron entry, systemd unit referencing /var/tmp/.xs), port-9000 callbacks to C2, and any SCP traffic to 38.242.204.245.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 587
| where RemoteUrl =~ "smtp.gmail.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".gmail.com"
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["mailrelay01","mailrelay02"]))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationPort == 587
  | where DestinationHostName has "smtp.gmail.com" or DestinationDnsDomain has "gmail.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstPortNumber == 587
  | where DstHostname has "smtp.gmail.com" or DstDomain has "gmail.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstHost=DstHostname, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetProto=NetworkProtocol)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SCP exfiltration of PCPJack proxy lists to downstream collector 38.242.204.245 AIActions on Objectives High
PCPJack syncs the verified-proxy list every five minutes via SCP to 38.242.204.245. Hunt for SSH/SCP/rsync connections to this IP, or process events showing scp/sftp invoking this destination on Linux beacons. Rationale: 38.242.204.245 is the named downstream collector receiving five-minute SCP syncs; pairing the IP with scp/rsync command-line keeps FP low. Confirmed by Hunt.io. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ops team using 38.x ranges for backup destinations (very rare for this specific IP)
  • SOC researcher actively probing the IOC from a known investigative host
  • Threat-intel pipeline pulling the IP for indicator enrichment
  • Backup job whose configuration is misconfigured to a typo'd destination
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/lib/backup/" and AccountName !in~ ("backupsvc","veeamsvc")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source host is not a sanctioned backup origin; capture full scp/rsync command line and the parent process. Expect the parent to be the Sliver implant or a deployer script. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, rotate SSH keys present on the host, block 38.242.204.245 at perimeter, snapshot for forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: extract the SSH known_hosts / authorized_keys, search for /var/tmp/.xs persistence, hunt across the fleet for any other host that has scp'd to the same collector.

PCPJack hidden Chisel implant drop at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux AIInstallation High
On the victim side the Sliver/Chisel binary is dropped as the hidden dot-prefixed file /var/tmp/.xs. Detect creation of this exact path, or any executable written to /var/tmp/ whose name starts with '.', then chmod'd +x. Rationale: /var/tmp/.xs is an exact path called out in the article as the persistence location for the Sliver/Chisel binary. Filtering well-known dot dirs keeps FPs minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user creating .swp/.swo Vim swap files in /var/tmp (mostly excluded by extension)
  • systemd-tmpfiles pruning sweeping in dot-prefixed lockfiles
  • Build pipeline using /var/tmp/.cache or /var/tmp/.npm style scratch directories
  • Sanctioned admin debug script dropping a dotfile for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vim","vi","nvim","systemd-tmpfiles") and not (FileName endswith ".swp" or FileName endswith ".swo")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull SHA256 of the dropped file and hash-check against VT/internal TI; identify the parent process and user that created the file. Step 2 — Contain: kill the implant process, quarantine the binary, isolate the host, rotate credentials present on the host, revoke cloud-instance IAM role session if compromised. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate cron and systemd persistence referencing /var/tmp/.xs, check for Chisel tunnel listeners on 10000-14999, and check fleet for the same file path and hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/"
| where FileName startswith "." and FileName !in~ (".X11-unix",".ICE-unix",".font-unix")
| extend IsXs = iif(FolderPath == "/var/tmp/.xs" or FileName == ".xs", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, IsXs
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/var/tmp/"
| where TargetFileName startswith "." and TargetFileName !in~ (".X11-unix",".ICE-unix",".font-unix")
| extend IsXs = iif(TargetFilePath == "/var/tmp/.xs" or TargetFileName == ".xs", "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, IsXs
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PCPJack SOCKS5 listener bound to deterministic port 10000-14999 on Linux AICommand & Control Medium
The deployer derives each beacon's SOCKS5 proxy port from an MD5 of its Sliver UUID, mapped to 10000-14999. Hunt for newly-bound listeners in that port range on Linux servers, especially when the listener is a non-standard binary in /var/tmp or /tmp. Rationale: The 10000-14999 SOCKS5 port range is explicitly called out and derived from MD5(UUID); restricting to listeners spawned from /var/tmp or /tmp narrows it to PCPJack-likely cases. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application servers using ephemeral high ports for legitimate microservices
  • Kubernetes NodePort services that fall in the 10000-14999 band
  • Developer running a local web server / proxy out of /tmp during testing
  • Monitoring agent that opens a transient debug port from /tmp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/lib/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/opt/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/snap/"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the listening process binary path and hash; confirm it's not part of an approved app inventory. Look for sibling Chisel binaries on the host. Step 2 — Contain: kill the listener, isolate the host, block 213.136.80.73 and 38.242.204.245 egress. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the binary's hash across the fleet, examine cron/systemd persistence, look for the chisel_verifier.py-style 60-second cycle of port probes from C2.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ListeningConnectionCreated","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| where LocalPort between (10000 .. 14999)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection in ("Inbound","Listen")
| where SrcPortNumber between (10000 .. 14999) or DstPortNumber between (10000 .. 14999)
| extend Port = coalesce(SrcPortNumber, DstPortNumber)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), DistinctPorts=dcount(Port), PortList=make_set(Port,50), Connections=count() by DvcHostname, EventVendor, EventProduct
| where DistinctPorts >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @SourcePort:[10000 TO 14999]) OR (source:linux.auditd @network.client.port:[10000 TO 14999] @process.executable.path:(\/var\/tmp\/* OR \/tmp\/.*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkListenIP4 LocalPort>=10000 LocalPort<=14999
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(var\/)?tmp\//i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/\.[^\/]+$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, LocalPort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.src) as src from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_port>=10000 All_Traffic.src_port<=14999 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_port host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats values(src_port) as ports dc(src_port) as port_count by src | where port_count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.src) as src from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_port>=10000 All_Traffic.src_port<=14999 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_port host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats values(src_port) as ports dc(src_port) as port_count by src | where port_count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
PCPJack exit-IP enrichment lookups to api.ipify.org and ip-api.com from Linux workloads AIReconnaissance Medium
After SMTP-gate verification PCPJack enriches each proxy with exit IP, country, and ASN via api.ipify.org and ip-api.com. Linux servers calling these enrichment services back-to-back (especially right after suspicious SMTP probing) are likely PCPJack-converted relays. Rationale: api.ipify.org and ip-api.com are named in the article as the enrichment path PCPJack uses to label proxies. Two distinct lookups from the same host is a strong PCPJack-shape signal. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1016 T1590.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Geolocation library bundled with a SaaS app legitimately checking exit IP
  • CI runner verifying its outbound IP for IP-allowlist validation
  • Personal-use script (curl ifconfig.me) by an admin
  • VPN client checking effective public IP after dial-up
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (dynamic(["curl","wget"])) or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the process making the call and whether it lives in /var/tmp or /tmp; correlate with same-host SMTP probes to smtp.gmail.com:587. Step 2 — Contain: if the process is the PCPJack implant, kill it, quarantine /var/tmp/.xs, isolate the host. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound to 213.136.80.73, SCP to 38.242.204.245, and Chisel listeners in 10000-14999.
let Enrichers = dynamic(["api.ipify.org","ip-api.com","ipinfo.io","ifconfig.me","icanhazip.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (Enrichers) or RemoteUrl has_any (Enrichers)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), HostsHit=make_set(RemoteUrl,10), Hits=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where array_length(HostsHit) >= 2 or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| order by FirstSeen desc
let Enrichers = dynamic(["api.ipify.org","ip-api.com","ipinfo.io","ifconfig.me","icanhazip.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DnsQuery in~ (Enrichers) or DnsQuery has_any (Enrichers)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, EventVendor, EventProduct),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where HttpHostName in~ (Enrichers) or Url has_any (Enrichers)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Lookups=make_set(Query,10), Hits=count() by Host, SrcIP
| where array_length(Lookups) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user

Stata binary spawning OS shell (CVE-2026-47708 stata-mcp log_file_name injection) AIExploitation High
Detects the Stata executable (or its Linux/macOS variants) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash/python child processes. This is the direct exploitation signal for CVE-2026-47708, where an attacker injects Stata's `shell` command via the unsanitised log_file_name parameter on the MCP `stata_do` tool, breaking out of the `log using "..."` string to execute arbitrary OS commands. Rationale: The article states the injection breaks out of the Stata `log using "..."` string so that `shell <cmd>` is interpreted as a Stata command, which then spawns an OS shell. Stata processes (stata.exe, stata-mp.exe, stata-se.exe, stata-be.exe, xstata variants) legitimately almost never spawn cmd/powershell/sh/bash/python children, so the parent-child pivot from the article's exploitation primitive is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory body (GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644) and the linked fix commit which confirms log_file_name was interpolated raw into the Stata command string. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644 • https://github.com/SepineTam/stata-mcp/commit/e6f945941ae0c7cf5e74a428e0b3dc82b396382f • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher do-files that legitimately call Stata's `shell` command to run git/make/system tooling
  • Stata's built-in `python` integration where researchers intentionally exit to a Python interpreter
  • Local development of stata-mcp itself where the developer is testing tool invocations
  • Stata batch wrappers (e.g. Stata-launch scripts via cmd.exe) where cmd.exe is briefly used to set environment before invoking stata — appears as stata→cmd in reverse direction (parent flip)
  • Defender ASR/EDR sensor self-test scripts that intentionally walk every parent-child combination
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","make ","type ","dir ","ls -") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".do")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine of the child shell and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the Stata parent; check whether the Stata cmdline references a `.do` file path that came from an MCP / stata-mcp tool invocation, and whether the child shell command line contains data-exfil patterns (curl/wget/nc/Invoke-WebRequest, base64, /tmp/, /dev/tcp/). Confirm the installed `stata-mcp` pip package version on the host — anything <1.17.3 is vulnerable. Step 2 — Contain: if the shell child issued network/file actions, isolate the host via Defender machine action / EDR network-isolate; kill the parent Stata PID and the stata-mcp Python wrapper process; rotate any credentials the Stata process had filesystem access to. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the parent Stata PID's file writes (UC2 below) for `.log` files with shell metacharacters in the filename; pivot on the stata-mcp wrapper's parent (often python.exe / uvx / pipx) and search for inbound MCP requests carrying `log_file_name
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("stata.exe","stata-mp.exe","stata-se.exe","stata-be.exe","xstata.exe","xstata-mp.exe","xstata-se.exe","stata","stata-mp","stata-se","stata-be")
| where FileName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","zsh.exe","bash","sh","zsh","python.exe","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("stata.exe","stata-mp.exe","stata-se.exe","stata-be.exe","xstata.exe","xstata-mp.exe","xstata-se.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","python.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects Stata executables spawning command shells, indicating likely exploitation of CVE-2026-47708 in stata-mcp where the log_file_name parameter is interpolated unsanitised into a Stata command, permitting Stata `shell` command injection.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644
  - https://github.com/SepineTam/stata-mcp/commit/e6f945941ae0c7cf5e74a428e0b3dc82b396382f

  - attack.execution

  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\stata.exe'
      - '\stata-mp.exe'
      - '\stata-se.exe'
      - '\stata-be.exe'
      - '\xstata.exe'
      - '\xstata-mp.exe'

Stata-authored log file written with shell metacharacters or path traversal in filename (CVE-2026-47708) AIExploitation High
Detects file writes by Stata or the stata-mcp Python wrapper where the target `.log` filename contains shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&`, backtick, single/double quotes) or path traversal (`..`). The article shows the PoC produces a literal log file whose filename contains the injected payload — even if the `shell` portion fails, the file artifact itself is a deterministic exploitation footprint. Rationale: The article's PoC explicitly shows the generated path becomes `<log_dir>/'; shell echo pwned > /tmp/pwned.txt; '.log` — i.e. the log filename literally contains a semicolon, single-quote, and redirection metacharacters, and (per `generate_log_file` having no path-traversal guard) may also contain `..`. Both observations come directly from the article's source-code excerpts and PoC. Filtering DeviceFileEvents to Stata/Python writers with `.log` extension narrows scope to near-zero baseline, and the regex on metacharacters/traversal isolates the exploitation artefact from any legitimate workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644 • https://github.com/SepineTam/stata-mcp/commit/e6f945941ae0c7cf5e74a428e0b3dc82b396382f
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researchers using single-quote in legitimate log filenames (e.g. `obama'speech.log`) — uncommon
  • Stata batch runs where the dataset name embedded into the log filename happens to contain a hyphen-prefixed value that looks like `..` (e.g. `panel..2024.log`)
  • Test fixtures inside the stata-mcp source tree that exercise the (now-fixed) parsing path
  • CI runners that intentionally fuzz the log_file_name parameter post-patch as a regression test
  • Backup/sync tools (rsync, OneDrive) writing `.log` artefacts with versioned suffixes that include quote characters
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFileName matches regex @"^panel\.\.20[0-9]{2}\.log$" or FolderPath has "\\stata-mcp\\tests\\fixtures\\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the full TargetFileName and FolderPath; reconstruct the original `log_file_name` payload the attacker sent to the MCP `stata_do` tool. Pull all sibling file activity (especially writes to /tmp/, %TEMP%, or anywhere outside the configured Stata log_file_path) from the same InitiatingProcessId — path-traversal in the same payload often writes a second file at an arbitrary location. Check the host's installed stata-mcp version (`pip show stata-mcp`) — vulnerable is <1.17.3. Step 2 — Contain: kill the Stata + stata-mcp wrapper processes; quarantine the malformed .log file and any second-payload files for IR; restrict the MCP server's listener (typically a local HTTP/stdio endpoint) until upgraded to ≥1.17.3. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessId to find any child shells (UC1) and any outbound network connections within the next 60s; search the MCP server's request logs (if proxied) for `log_file_name` values containing quote/semicolon/newline characters; expand

| where FileName endswith ".log"
| where FileName matches regex @"[;|&`'\"]|\.\."
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("stata_mcp","stata-mcp","log_file_name")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath

ImFileEvent

Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm exfiltration to t.m-kosche.com OpenTelemetry endpoint AIActions on Objectives High
Detects DNS/HTTP egress to the TeamPCP exfiltration C2 at t.m-kosche.com, where stolen creds are POSTed to /api/public/otel/v1/traces masquerading as OpenTelemetry traffic. High-fidelity because the FQDN and URI path are unique to this campaign and corroborated by Wiz, Snyk and Socket. Rationale: Pivots on the exact exfil FQDN (t.m-kosche.com) and the unique OpenTelemetry-disguise URI path (/api/public/otel/v1/traces) called out in Wiz, Snyk and Socket write-ups of the same Mini Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP wave that published @cap-js/openapi@1.4.1 on 2026-05-19. Both strings are unambiguous IOCs with no benign collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://socket.dev/blog/sap-cap-npm-packages-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/mini-shai-hulud-pushes-malicious-antv.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1071.001

  • Threat-intel feed validation jobs that probe IOC domains
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ logging the blocked query (treat as confirmation, not FP)
  • Vulnerability scanner crawling NIST/GHSA references
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("GHSA-jpvj","advisories/GHSA"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the resolving/connecting process is node, npm, npx, yarn, pnpm or bun (not chrome/edge browsing the IOC article). Pull the parent process tree and the package.json directory walk back to identify which npm scope (@cap-js, @antv, @lint-md, etc.) preinstall fired. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host from network, kill node/bun, block t.m-kosche.com at proxy/DNS-firewall, immediately revoke ALL credentials reachable from that workstation (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/Azure/GCP keys, SSH private keys, kubeconfig, Vault tokens). Assume creds are already compromised — rotate, don't audit. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host's npm registry mirror logs for `npm publish` calls (worm propagation), and on GitHub audit log for new public repos created by the developer's PAT in the last 14 days (backup exfil channel).

Bun runtime spawned by npm/node preinstall hook (TeamPCP setup.mjs loader) AIInstallation High
Detects the Mini Shai-Hulud execution chain where the compromised npm preinstall hook in @cap-js/openapi (and sibling packages) invokes the Bun JavaScript runtime to load setup.mjs → execution.js. Bun is rarely a child of npm/node in enterprise environments and is the campaign's signature loader. Rationale: Wiz and Socket both document the bun-runtime loader chain (preinstall→setup.mjs→bun→execution.js) as the Mini Shai-Hulud signature. Bun being spawned by npm/node is rare outside dedicated Bun shops, and pairing it with the `preinstall` / `setup.mjs` / `execution.js` strings caught in cmdline lifts confidence dramatically. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://socket.dev/blog/sap-cap-npm-packages-supply-chain-attack • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://safedep.io/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-314-npm-packages-compromised/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer monorepo that uses Bun as a faster install/test runner and shells out from npm-orchestrated scripts
  • CI pipeline that intentionally runs `npm test` → `bun run` for performance
  • Bun installer itself (`bun install`) running during initial dev-environment setup, parented by node bootstrap
  • Vendor SDK that bundles a Bun-based build step (e.g., some Tauri/Bun hybrid projects)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "bun install" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","zsh") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the full process tree (bun's grandparent should be the originating npm/yarn/pnpm install command); pull the working directory and search it for node_modules/@cap-js/openapi/package.json containing version 1.4.1 or any other Mini Shai-Hulud-listed scope (@antv, @lint-md, @openclaw-cn, @starmind, @cap-js, mbt). Step 2 — Contain: kill the bun and parent npm processes, network-isolate the host, snapshot disk and memory if forensics are in scope. Block bun.exe via WDAC/AppLocker on developer images that have no legitimate Bun use case. Step 3 — Hunt: query the package registry mirror or proxy for downloads of any Mini Shai-Hulud-listed package in the last 30 days across all dev hosts, and correlate against this UC to find every workstation that ran the loader. Rotate every credential the affected developer could touch.
// TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud: Bun spawned from npm preinstall
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName =~ "bun"
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","npm-cli.js","node","npm","yarn","pnpm","npx"))
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","setup.mjs","execution.js")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud: Bun spawned from npm preinstall (Sentinel — SecurityEvent 4688 + ASIM)
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/bun"
  | where (ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe","/npm","/node","/yarn","/pnpm","/npx"))
       or CommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js","preinstall")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="SecurityEvent"),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetProcessName endswith "bun.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "/bun"
  | where (ParentProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe"))
       or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js")
       or ParentProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="ImProcessCreate")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime Spawned by npm Preinstall (Mini Shai-Hulud Loader)
id: b2c3d4e5-f6a7-4901-bcde-2345678901bc
description: Detects the Bun JavaScript runtime spawned as a child of npm/node/yarn/pnpm — the loader pattern used by TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud worm (setup.mjs/execution.js) including @cap-js/openapi@1.4.1.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jpvj-wpmj-h7rv
  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '/bun'
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\npx.exe'
      - '/npm'
      - '/node'
      - '/yarn'
      - '/pnpm'
      - '/npx'
  selection_cmdline:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'setup.mjs'

falsepositives:
  - Developers intentionally using Bun as a build accelerator in monorepos
  - CI runners that invoke Bun from a node-based orchestrator
level: high
source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:1 AND @Image:(*\bun.exe OR *\Bun.exe OR *\BUN.EXE OR */bun) AND (@ParentImage:(*\npm.exe OR *\NPM.EXE OR *\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe OR *\npx.exe OR */npm OR */node OR */yarn OR */pnpm OR */npx) OR @CommandLine:(*setup.mjs* OR *execution.js* OR *preinstall*) OR @ParentCommandLine:(*preinstall* OR *setup.mjs*))

Mini Shai-Hulud payload SHA256 on disk (7c24b4d9...e627144e8b) AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based detection for the specific malicious payload binary tied to @cap-js/openapi@1.4.1 in GHSA-jpvj-wpmj-h7rv. Catches the file at write-time (DeviceFileEvents) and at any subsequent execution attempt — definitive identification with effectively zero FP risk. Rationale: Direct SHA256/SHA1 IOC pivots from the GHSA advisory itself. Hash-on-disk and hash-on-execution coverage closes both the install and the run pathway; multi-table union catches it whether the file lands during npm install, gets loaded as a DLL/module, or runs as a process. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jpvj-wpmj-h7rv • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sample stored in a malware-analysis VM / sandbox
  • Forensic disk image of an affected workstation mounted for investigation
  • EDR / AV vendor signature database update containing the hash as a definition (file path will give it away)
  • Threat-intel-platform ingestion of the IOC into a flat-file IOC repo on a SOC analyst's box
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has_any (@"\Quarantine\", @"\Malware\", @"\Sandbox\", @"\IOC-store\", @"\samples\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the file path (real victim files land under node_modules/@cap-js/openapi/... or a sibling Mini Shai-Hulud scope's node_modules; sandbox/quarantine paths are obvious). Identify the InitiatingProcess that wrote the file (should be npm/node/yarn/pnpm/bun for a real infection). Step 2 — Contain: kill the file's writer + any running process matching the hash, network-isolate the host, snapshot disk + memory. Revoke every credential that workstation could reach — assume harvest and exfil completed before detection (the payload runs within seconds of preinstall). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the SHA256 across DeviceFileEvents / FileWritten enterprise-wide for the last 60d to scope all infected hosts, and across DeviceProcessEvents to find any cached install that has executed since.
// Mini Shai-Hulud payload hash IOCs from GHSA-jpvj-wpmj-h7rv
let badSha256 = dynamic(["7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b"]);
let badSha1 = dynamic(["d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSha256) or SHA1 in (badSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, Source="DeviceFileEvents"),
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSha256) or SHA1 in (badSha1) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (badSha256) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (badSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1,
            ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            FileOriginUrl="", FileOriginIP="", Source="DeviceProcessEvents"),
(DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSha256) or SHA1 in (badSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1,
            InitiatingProcessFileName=InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            FileOriginUrl="", FileOriginIP="", Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
// Mini Shai-Hulud payload hash IOCs (Sentinel)
let badSha256 = dynamic(["7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b"]);
let badSha1 = dynamic(["d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
  | where TargetFileSHA256 in (badSha256) or TargetFileSHA1 in (badSha1) or Hash in (badSha256) or Hash in (badSha1)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername,
            FileName=TargetFileName, FolderPath=TargetFilePath,
            SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1,
            Process=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImFileEvent"),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSha256) or SHA1 in (badSha1) or Hash in (badSha256) or Hash in (badSha1)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername,
            FileName=TargetProcessName, FolderPath=TargetProcessName,
            SHA256, SHA1, Process=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, Source="ImProcessCreate"),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
  | where FileHash in (badSha256) or FileHash in (badSha1)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, Account=SourceUserName,
            FileName, FolderPath=FilePath, SHA256=FileHash, SHA1=FileHash,
            Process=ProcessName, CommandLine=Message, Source="CommonSecurityLog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud/SSH/npm credential file access by Node or Bun during npm install AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the credential harvesting stage of Mini Shai-Hulud: Node or Bun (when spawned within an npm install context) reading developer secret stores — ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/.ssh/id_*, gh hosts.yml, kubeconfig, .docker/config.json, Vault tokens. These files are read by the malware to enumerate cloud/CI credentials before exfil. Rationale: Wiz, Snyk, Socket and Unit42 all enumerate the same harvest target set (AWS/Azure/GCP/Kubernetes/GitHub/npm/SSH/Vault). Detecting node or bun in install-context fanning out across ≥3 of these distinct cred file types within a single process group is the highest-signal behavioural pivot the malware leaves before exfiltrating to t.m-kosche.com. Anti-pattern-aware: threshold and process gate suppress benign single-file reads (npm reads ~/.npmrc every install on its own). Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://socket.dev/blog/sap-cap-npm-packages-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AWS CDK / Pulumi / Serverless framework legitimately reading ~/.aws/credentials during deploy
  • GitHub CLI extension or git-credential-manager being invoked from a node-based pre-commit hook
  • Developer running `npm run deploy` that touches kube + docker + aws creds in sequence
  • Test harness that reads .npmrc, kubeconfig and .docker/config.json to validate dev environment setup
  • Node-based dotfile manager / chezmoi-style tool legitimately enumerating dotfiles
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-cdk","@aws-cdk","pulumi","serverless","@serverless","sst","chezmoi","git-credential-manager") and PathsTouched !has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full set of paths touched within the InitiatingProcessId window — true positives almost always span >3 distinct cred ecosystems (AWS+SSH+npm+GitHub), legitimate tools usually touch one. Correlate the host against UC1 (t.m-kosche.com egress) and UC2 (bun spawned by npm) — any two of three confirms incident. Step 2 — Contain: revoke EVERY credential matching the touched files (rotate AWS keys, regenerate SSH keypairs, revoke GitHub PAT + npm token, regenerate kubeconfigs). Isolate host, snapshot, do not wipe — preserve evidence of what was harvested. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate the developer's recent npm installs (npm-debug.log, ~/.npm/_logs) to identify the entry-point package; cross-reference to the Mini Shai-Hulud package list and notify any downstream consumers if the developer published packages of their own in the last 14 days.
// Mini Shai-Hulud credential harvest: node/bun touching multiple secret stores during install
let credPaths = dynamic([
  @"\.aws\credentials", @"/.aws/credentials",
  @"\.aws\config", @"/.aws/config",
  @"\.npmrc", @"/.npmrc",
  @"\.ssh\id_", @"/.ssh/id_",
  @"\.ssh\known_hosts", @"/.ssh/known_hosts",
  @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml", @"/.config/gh/hosts.yml",
  @"\.kube\config", @"/.kube/config",
  @"\.docker\config.json", @"/.docker/config.json",
  @".vault-token",
  @"\AppData\Roaming\gcloud\credentials.db", @"/.config/gcloud/credentials.db",
  @"\.azure\msal_token_cache", @"/.azure/msal_token_cache"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileOpenInfo","FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","npm.exe","npm","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","setup.mjs","execution.js","npm ci","npm i ")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (credPaths) or FileName has_any (credPaths)
| summarize HitCount = count(), PathsTouched = make_set(FolderPath, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
  by DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where HitCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
// Mini Shai-Hulud credential harvest via ASIM file events
let credPaths = dynamic([
  @"\.aws\credentials", @"/.aws/credentials",
  @"\.aws\config", @"/.aws/config",
  @"\.npmrc", @"/.npmrc",
  @"\.ssh\id_", @"/.ssh/id_",
  @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml", @"/.config/gh/hosts.yml",
  @"\.kube\config", @"/.kube/config",
  @"\.docker\config.json", @"/.docker/config.json",
  @".vault-token",
  @"/.config/gcloud/credentials.db",
  @"/.azure/msal_token_cache"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","setup.mjs","execution.js")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (credPaths) or TargetFileName has_any (credPaths)
| summarize HitCount = count(), PathsTouched = make_set(TargetFilePath, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
  by Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where HitCount >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537") or SHA1 in~ ("7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537") or MD5 in~ ("7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537") or SHA1 in~ ("7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537") or MD5 in~ ("7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7c24b4d9a8f448832f3752d7f67dcdbf1b7f0f41e10bf633efa175e627144e8b", "d78c25443ec4a0d7f0a85776461f3b1163132537"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-8whc-2wmv-ww35: WWBN AVideo: Unauthenticated Stored DOM Cross-Site Scripting via Per-Client Metadata Broadcast in YPTSocket Plugin

GitHub Security Advisories
2026-06-04 3 use cases 2 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

WWBN AVideo: Unauthenticated Stored DOM Cross-Site Scripting via Per-Client Metadata Broadcast in YPTSocket Plugin

ATT&CKT1190 T1539

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AVideo YPTSocket plugin XSS injection via webSocketSelfURI/page_title query strings · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-8whc-2wmv-ww35: WWBN AVideo: Unauthenticated Stored DOM C
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
AVideo YPTSocket plugin XSS injection via webSocketSelfURI/page_title query strings AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated exploitation of GHSA-8whc-2wmv-ww35 in WWBN AVideo by detecting HTTP requests to the YPTSocket token endpoint or WebSocket upgrade carrying HTML/JS payloads in the webSocketSelfURI or page_title query parameters. The payload is then broadcast to any admin viewing a page that renders the YPTSocket debug panel. Rationale: Anchored on the exact endpoint path /plugin/YPTSocket/ and the two attacker-controlled parameters (webSocketSelfURI, page_title) named in functions.php:21-24 and MessageSQLiteV2.php:91/110, combined with URL-encoded and raw HTML/JS payload tokens (including the article's String.fromCharCode evasion). Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory text and the AVideo repo paths cited in the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8whc-2wmv-ww35 • https://github.com/WWBN/AVideo
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA/security teams pentesting the YPTSocket plugin (legitimate XSS test payloads)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Burp Suite, Nuclei, ZAP) probing AVideo with HTML/JS canary payloads
  • Bug-bounty researchers replaying the PoC against staging
  • Legitimate AVideo dashboards passing rich page titles that happen to contain '<' (rare — utf8_encode source values normally don't carry HTML)
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has_any ("Burp", "Nuclei", "ZAP", "sqlmap", "nikto") and SrcIp !in ("<internal_pentest_ranges>")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull all hits on /plugin/YPTSocket/getWebSocket.json.php and the WebSocket upgrade with these parameters in the last 48h; URL-decode the query string and identify the actual JS payload, source IP, and User-Agent. Confirm whether the AVideo instance has the YPTSocket plugin enabled and debugSocket=true (the vulnerable default). Step 2 — Contain: block the offending source IP at the WAF/edge, disable the YPTSocket plugin or set debugSocket=false until patched (upgrade composer:WWBN/AVideo above 29.0), and force-rotate admin session cookies and CSRF tokens for any admin who was logged in during the window. Step 3 — Hunt: review admin-context API calls (user/role mutations, password changes, plugin enable/disable, content edits) from admin session IDs that overlap with the broadcast window; pivot on AdminUser browser sessions to outbound exfil to attacker-controlled domains in DeviceNetworkEvents.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/plugin/YPTSocket/"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("webSocketSelfURI=", "page_title=")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("%3Cimg", "%3Cscript", "onerror%3D", "onload%3D", "%3Csvg", "javascript%3A", "String.fromCharCode", "%3Ciframe", "<img", "<script", "onerror=", "onload=")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectTokens = dynamic(["%3Cimg","%3Cscript","onerror%3D","onload%3D","%3Csvg","javascript%3A","String.fromCharCode","%3Ciframe","<img","<script","onerror=","onload=","fromCharCode"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/plugin/YPTSocket/"
    | where (csUriQuery has "webSocketSelfURI=" or csUriQuery has "page_title=")
    | where csUriQuery has_any (SuspectTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=cIP, Method=csMethod, Uri=strcat(csUriStem,"?",csUriQuery), Status=scStatus, UserAgent=csUserAgent),
  (AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where CsUriStem has "/plugin/YPTSocket/"
    | where (CsUriQuery has "webSocketSelfURI=" or CsUriQuery has "page_title=")
    | where CsUriQuery has_any (SuspectTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=CsHost, SrcIp=CIp, Method=CsMethod, Uri=strcat(CsUriStem,"?",CsUriQuery), Status=ScStatus, UserAgent=UserAgent),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/plugin/YPTSocket/"
    | where RequestURL has_any ("webSocketSelfURI=","page_title=")
    | where RequestURL has_any (SuspectTokens)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host=DestinationHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Method=RequestMethod, Uri=RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent=RequestClientApplication)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Reporting from Vegas: Networking, AI, and good boys
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos weekly prevalent malware SHA256 IOC sweep (Coinminer / Procpatcher / KMS activator) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Talos weekly prevalent malware SHA256 IOC sweep (Coinminer / Procpatcher / KMS activator) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts process executions and file writes matching the five SHA256 hashes Talos called out as the week's most prevalent malware in their 2026-06-04 newsletter telemetry roundup. Covers Win.Worm.Coinminer (VID001.exe), Win.Tool.Procpatcher (sample.exe), W32.C0AD494457-95 (f_000b97.html), and PUA.Win.Tool.Kmsactivator (AutoPico.exe). Rationale: Detection is grounded on the five SHA256 hashes Talos explicitly named in the 'Most prevalent malware files' block (VID001.exe Coinminer, sample.exe Procpatcher, f_000b97.html W32.C0AD494457-95, AutoPico.exe Kmsactivator, plus the fifth truncated entry). These are confirmed-bad per Talos detection names — file-reputation match is the highest-fidelity signal possible from this article. No external sources cross-checked: the IOC list is a weekly Talos telemetry snapshot from today's date with no second source yet published.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analysts intentionally detonating samples in a sandbox / malware-analysis VM (especially analysts retrieving Talos-flagged hashes for testing)
  • AutoPico.exe / KMS activator hash firing on unlicensed Windows installs (common in test/lab environments and unmanaged dev boxes)
  • f_000b97.html cached in browser cache directories from a benign visit — file write triggers without execution (review FolderPath for browser cache paths before escalating)
  • EDR vendor sample-collection / threat intel platforms (CrowdStrike, MDE attack surface reduction telemetry) pulling sample copies for analysis
  • Legitimate AV scanners writing the sample to quarantine — initiating process being the AV engine itself
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !contains "\\Sandbox\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","CSFalconService.exe","SenseIR.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the matching event's FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, and AccountName. If folder is a known sandbox/quarantine path (e.g. C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Quarantine, sandbox VM paths) or parent is an AV engine, downgrade. Confirm the Talos detection name from the case statement against the article's labelling. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response / CrowdStrike RTR network containment. Kill the live process tree; quarantine the file. For Coinminer (VID001.exe) check for persistence via Run keys and scheduled tasks; for Procpatcher review which process was patched (often AV/EDR tampering). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessParentFileName to find the delivery vector (browser download? email attachment? USB?). Sweep the rest of the fleet for the same SHA256 over 30 days and for the parent's hash. If KMS activator triggered, audit the host for other PUA / cracked software via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory.

let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SHA256 in (TalosMalwareHashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
              ParentFileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              Source = "DeviceProcessEvents";
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SHA256 in (TalosMalwareHashes)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
              ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
              ParentFileName = InitiatingProcessParentFileName, ParentCmd = "",
              Source = "DeviceFileEvents";
union ProcHits, FileHits

| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
