Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF exploitation attempt (CVE-2026-20230) AIExploitation Medium
Detects external or non-Jabber HTTP traffic to the Cisco Unified Communications Manager WebDialer Web Service path — the vulnerable component for CVE-2026-20230. Cisco confirmed WebDialer is the affected endpoint and is disabled by default, so any external POST/PUT/GET to /webdialer/ on a UCM listener (443/8443) is a high-fidelity exploitation indicator now that public PoC code from SSD Secure Disclosure is in the wild. Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable component named in the Cisco PSIRT advisory (WebDialer Web Service) rather than generic UCM traffic. Excludes Cisco Jabber/Webex desktop clients — the legitimate callers of /webdialer/ — to drop the realistic FP set. Confirmed against the Cisco advisory and BleepingComputer/SecurityWeek/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-ssrf-cXPnHcW • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisco-warns-of-critical-unified-cm-flaw-with-poc-exploit-code/ • https://www.securityweek.com/cisco-warns-of-available-poc-for-critical-unified-cm-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) probing CUCM web interfaces from corporate ranges
  • Custom in-house click-to-dial integration calling /webdialer/ from a CRM or helpdesk app
  • Cisco TAC remote troubleshooting via tunneled session
  • Pen-test engagement that hasn't been deconflicted
  • Legitimate user accessing WebDialer through a corporate VPN egress IP that looks external
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessusd.exe","qualysagent.exe","insightvm-agent.exe","tenable-agent.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1: Pull full request URI, body, and headers for the matching events and check Cisco UCM /var/log/active/tomcat/ for matching access entries with anomalous HTTP method / payload size. Confirm whether the source IP is on the approved CUCM admin allow-list. Step 2: Apply Cisco's interim mitigation — disable Cisco WebDialer Web Service via Cisco Unified Serviceability (Service Activation menu) until 14SU6 / 15SU5 is deployed. Block external 443/8443 ingress to UCM at the perimeter. Step 3: Hunt for post-exploit indicators on the UCM filesystem — unexpected file writes under /usr/local/cm/, /opt/cisco/, or /tmp/ owned by the tomcat/ccmservice account; new files in webapps/ paths; and unusual outbound connections from the UCM management interface.
let webdialer_paths = dynamic(["/webdialer/","/cmcip/","/webdialerservice/"]);
let legit_jabber_clients = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe","brave.exe","outlook.exe","lync.exe","teams.exe","jabber.exe","ciscojabber.exe","ciscowebexstart.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (443, 8443, 80)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (webdialer_paths)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (legit_jabber_clients)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| extend SrcIp = tostring(SourceIP)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIp))
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cisco Unified CM WebDialer SSRF Exploitation Attempt CVE-2026-20230
id: 7c4d5e9a-1b2f-4a3d-8e9c-0f1a2b3c4d5e
description: Detects HTTP requests to the Cisco Unified Communications Manager WebDialer Web Service from unexpected sources that may indicate SSRF exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-20230. WebDialer is disabled by default and is only normally accessed by Cisco Jabber / similar click-to-dial clients.
references:

Tiflux RMM MSI installer drop with lawdepotisland/lenwillfilenetwork malspam infrastructure AIInstallation High
Detects the Huntress-documented Tiflux campaign: an MSI installer for the Tiflux commercial RMM landing on a host that previously contacted the campaign's malspam infrastructure (businessservices@hg.lawdepotisland.com / lenwillfilenetwork.com). Distinct from a legitimate Tiflux MSP deployment because the install is preceded by traffic to those two domains. Rationale: Couples Huntress's two strongest IOCs from the May–June 2026 Tiflux writeup — the Tiflux MSI install pattern AND prior contact with the malspam staging domains (hg.lawdepotisland.com, lenwillfilenetwork.com) — into a single high-confidence correlation. Mere Tiflux presence is too noisy for orgs that legitimately use it; the malspam-domain precursor is what makes the install adversarial. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/tiflux-rmm-install • https://www.techradar.com/pro/security/hackers-abuse-ultravnc-splashtop-and-screenconnect-to-hijack-business-pcs
ATT&CKT1219 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Org legitimately adopting Tiflux as primary RMM where a user separately received marketing email from a similar-looking sender
  • Tiflux MSP onboarding visit where the technician's MSI deployment coincides with unrelated DNS lookups
  • Security tool/sandbox detonating Huntress's reference samples
  • Tiflux trial install by IT for evaluation
Response runbook
Step 1: Pull the originating email from EmailEvents for the host's user (SenderFromAddress containing lawdepotisland) and confirm the lure document — fake business service agreement per Huntress. Verify the MSI's SHA256 and code-signing certificate against Tiflux's legitimate publisher. Step 2: Isolate the host, kill tiflux* processes, remove the MSI-installed service, and block hg.lawdepotisland.com / lenwillfilenetwork.com at the proxy/DNS layer. Reset credentials for the user whose mailbox received the lure. Step 3: Hunt fleet-wide for the same Tiflux MSI hash and for subsequent installs of UltraVNC / Splashtop / ScreenConnect or the HwRwDrv.sys driver — Huntress reports those as the daisy-chained follow-on tooling.
let tiflux_install_window = 30d;
let malspam_domains = dynamic(["hg.lawdepotisland.com","lawdepotisland.com","lenwillfilenetwork.com"]);
let hosts_touched_malspam = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(tiflux_install_window)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (malspam_domains)
    | distinct DeviceId;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(tiflux_install_window)
| where (FileName =~ "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "tiflux") 
     or FileName has_any ("tiflux.exe","tiflux-agent.exe","TifluxAgent.exe")
| where DeviceId in (hosts_touched_malspam)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let tiflux_install_window = 30d;

let hosts_touched_malspam = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(tiflux_install_window)
    | where Name has_any (malspam_domains)
    | distinct Computer;
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| extend ProcBase = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where (ProcBase == "msiexec.exe" and CommandLine has "tiflux") 
     or ProcBase in ("tiflux.exe","tiflux-agent.exe","tifluxagent.exe")
| where Computer in (hosts_touched_malspam)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) (@CommandLine:*tiflux* OR @Image:(*\\tiflux.exe OR *\\TifluxAgent.exe OR *\\tiflux-agent.exe) OR @Image:(*\\msiexec.exe OR *\\MsiExec.exe) AND @CommandLine:*tiflux*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\msiexec\.exe$/i CommandLine=/tiflux/i) OR ImageFileName=/\\(tiflux(-agent)?|TifluxAgent)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| eval campaign="Huntress-Tiflux-2026"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdlines values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parents from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="msiexec.exe" Processes.process="*tiflux*") OR Processes.process_name IN ("tiflux.exe","tiflux-agent.exe","TifluxAgent.exe") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name

| eval campaign="Huntress-Tiflux-2026"
HwRwDrv.sys vulnerable driver load — Tiflux campaign BYOVD privilege escalation AIExploitation High
Detects the load of HwRwDrv.sys, the outdated/expired-cert kernel driver Huntress observed bundled inside the Tiflux installer for privilege elevation. Independent of the Tiflux install vector — this driver is a known BYOVD primitive and any load is suspicious unless an explicit IT-approved use exists. Rationale: HwRwDrv.sys is the specific BYOVD driver Huntress called out for the Tiflux campaign — narrow, named, low-FP. The driver carries an expired cert, so a load is itself anomalous regardless of the loader. Confirmed against the Huntress writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/tiflux-rmm-install
ATT&CKT1068 T1543.003 T1014
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy HP/Hewlett-Packard hardware utility that bundled HwRwDrv.sys (the driver originated from a Hewlett-Packard rapid-write tool) running on an unpatched workstation
  • Forensics/IR analyst loading the sample in a sandbox VM for triage
  • Red-team engagement using the same vulnerable driver
  • Vendor diagnostic toolkit that hasn't been refreshed and still ships the driver
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Hewlett-Packard" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\HP\\"
Response runbook
Step 1: Confirm the driver's SHA256 and signing cert validity period against Microsoft's vulnerable-driver blocklist; capture the loader process and its parent. Step 2: Isolate the host and remove the driver — use `sc delete` for the associated service and delete the .sys from %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\; ensure Microsoft's vulnerable driver blocklist is enabled (HVCI) fleet-wide. Step 3: Pivot to the loader's parent process tree to determine the installation vector — confirm whether Tiflux MSI dropped it (link to UC2) and hunt for follow-on persistence (UltraVNC, ScreenConnect, Splashtop services / autoruns) added in the same window.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HwRwDrv.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID in (6, 7)
| where EventData has "HwRwDrv.sys"
| extend ImageLoaded = tostring(EventData.ImageLoaded), Signature = tostring(EventData.Signature), SignatureStatus = tostring(EventData.SignatureStatus), Hashes = tostring(EventData.Hashes), LoaderImage = tostring(EventData.Image)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, LoaderImage, ImageLoaded, Signature, SignatureStatus, Hashes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

logsource:

ENDPOINT

| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime count values(ImageLoaded) as drivers values(Signature) as sigs values(SignatureStatus) as sig_status values(Hashes) as hashes by host, User, ProcessGuid, Image

DriveSurge zTDS infrastructure connections (ClickFix / FakeUpdates delivery) AIDelivery High
Detects connections to the DriveSurge IAB's zTDS traffic-distribution infrastructure and the campaign's IOC IP/domain set published in Silent Push's June 2026 writeup. Hosts hit zTDS through redirection from compromised high-reputation websites, so the originating process is typically a legitimate browser — that's the whole point of the detection. Rationale: All eight domains and four IPs are the article's extracted IOC set for the DriveSurge IAB and zTDS infrastructure — high-fidelity match. Because compromised legitimate sites do the redirecting, the hit will typically come from a normal browser process, which is intended behaviour for this detection.
ATT&CKT1189 T1608.006 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher's sandbox VM intentionally hitting zTDS for sample triage
  • Stale browser cache hit from a previously-compromised legitimate site that has since been remediated
  • IOC-feed validation tool generating test queries
  • User clicking a benign redirect through a domain that briefly shared infra with the campaign
  • Security-vendor crawler doing IOC sweeping from a corporate IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatresearch.exe","sandbox-driver.exe","misp-import.exe","cuckoo-agent.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1: Identify the originating browser process and the referrer URL — the referrer is the compromised high-reputation site that performed the silent redirect. Pull the user's browser history for the same window to map the click path. Step 2: Sinkhole/block the eight domains and four IPs at the DNS and perimeter layer; isolate the host and check for a ClickFix prompt (clipboard contained mshta/powershell command) or a FakeUpdates download in browser downloads/Temp. Step 3: Submit the referrer (compromised site) to Silent Push and notify the site owner; hunt fleet-wide for explorer.exe-spawned mshta.exe / powershell.exe within 5 minutes of the zTDS hit (ClickFix follow-on) and for SectopRAT / ACRStealer indicators that the article cites as the DriveSurge downstream payload.
let drivesurge_domains = dynamic(["ztds.info","beacontrace.bond","webgleam.info","check.first-node.rocks","cptoptious.com","banerpanel.live","testio.ecartdev.com","captioto.com"]);
let drivesurge_ips = dynamic(["91.92.240.127","46.226.166.57","147.45.42.200","147.45.42.205"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (drivesurge_ips) 
     or RemoteUrl has_any (drivesurge_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

(CommonSecurityLog

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20230")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-20230")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-20230")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AuditLogs

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")

| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a") or SHA1 in~ ("90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a") or MD5 in~ ("90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a") or SHA1 in~ ("90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a") or MD5 in~ ("90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["90aecb370dfb1a99a1f7de0a9c6842ab1b664521fddea16b0ec9a91f322646fc", "7aa15de93cf85729ddf970e8d7897f69ece3ca29608f73e784a9ba40c9cea18d", "8ecc7108cd679316bf5900e84f19b256dc399902cdede646493f502ac872cc1a", "e1ce4e6222396a58d13dddfe64c1cc21f1632bcbe11d1867d44bab4fc646883a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma npm Supply Chain Attack: Self-Spreading Worm via Phantom Gyp

StepSecurity
2026-06-04 5 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

self-replicating worm is spreading across the npm registry using binding.gyp, a file that triggers code execution during npm install without touching package.json scripts. The attack bypasses conventional security tools and has already compromised dozens of packages across multiple maintainer accounts.

ATT&CKT1027 T1190 T1195.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma npm Supply Chain Attack: Self-Spreading Worm via Phantom Gyp
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Claude Code GitHub Action Flaw Let One Malicious Issue Hijack Repositories

The Hacker News
2026-06-04 7 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A security researcher found a flaw in Anthropic's Claude Code GitHub Action that let an attacker take over vulnerable public repositories running it, with nothing more than a single opened GitHub issue. Because Anthropic's own action repo used the same workflow, a working attack could have pushed malicious code into the action itself and onto the projects downstream that pull it. RyotaK of GMO

Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner reads /proc/<pid>/environ (Claude Code prompt-injection cred-theft) AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact technique RyotaK used to weaponise the Claude Code GitHub Action: a prompt-injected issue body coaxes Claude into shelling out and dumping /proc/self/environ to harvest ANTHROPIC_API_KEY plus ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN / URL. Detection fires when any process under a self-hosted Actions runner ancestry reads /proc/*/environ. Not relevant to GitHub-hosted runners (no telemetry), only self-hosted Linux runner fleets. Rationale: Anchored on the exact exfil mechanic RyotaK described (Claude bypassing the naive /proc/self/environ guard) and bound to a self-hosted runner ancestry (Runner.Worker / _work/_actions / claude-code-action). v1.0.94 patches env-var scrubbing for child processes, so any post-patch hit on this rule on a self-hosted runner is highly indicative of either an unpatched action OR a bypass; pre-patch it is the primary IOC. Cross-checked against GMO Flatt Security writeup and Cybersecurity News article. Cross-checked against: • https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/claude-codes-github-actions-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/main/docs/security.md
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059.004 T1078.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer SSH'd into a self-hosted runner running `cat /proc/$$/environ` to debug a failing workflow's env
  • osquery / process-inspection tooling scanning /proc as part of inventory
  • Container runtime (containerd / docker) reading /proc/<pid>/environ during health-checks on the runner host
  • Custom workflow that legitimately inspects env vars for debugging (e.g. `printenv` substituted with `cat /proc/self/environ`)
  • Build tooling like `proot`/`fakeroot` enumerating /proc during sandboxing
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("osqueryd","containerd-shim","docker-runc","systemd-cgls","falcon-sensor")) and not(AccountName endswith "$") and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("printenv","--debug-env"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the InitiatingProcess tree on the runner host - confirm the parent chain traces to Runner.Worker → node executing actions/anthropics/claude-code-action. Pull the workflow run URL from the runner's _diag log and identify the triggering issue/PR number + actor. If the actor name ends in `[bot]` and the issue body contains an 'error message' / 'recovery procedure' / mentions of environ, treat as confirmed exploit. 2) CONTAIN: pause the self-hosted runner (`./svc.sh stop`), rotate ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, revoke the Claude Code GitHub App installation token and any GITHUB_TOKEN referenced in that workflow's logs, and freeze the runner host pending forensics. Pin the workflow's claude-code-action ref to ≥ v1.0.94 and remove `allowed_non_write_users: "*"`. 3) HUNT: search for prior issue comments posted by the action's bot account containing strings matching `[A-Z_]+=` or `ghs_` / `ghu_` / `gho_` / `eyJ` (JWT prefix) - those are leaked env dumps. Pivot on the OIDC sub claim / insta
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has "/environ"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","head","xxd","od","strings","tr","awk","grep","sed","tail","dd","sh","bash","python","python3","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Runner.Worker","_work/_actions","_work/_temp","claude-code-action","anthropics/claude-code")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/actions-runner/","/runner/_work/","_actions/anthropics")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "ProcessCreated"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/environ"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(/|^)(cat|head|xxd|od|strings|tr|awk|grep|sed|tail|dd|sh|bash|python3?|node)$"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("Runner.Worker","_work/_actions","_work/_temp","claude-code-action","anthropics/claude-code")
    or ParentProcessName has_any ("Runner.Worker","Runner.Listener")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runner Reads /proc/self/environ (Claude Code Injection)
id: 9c3a5e1f-2b88-4f51-8df1-9c12b3d2a17e
description: Detects a Linux process under a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner ancestry that reads /proc/<pid>/environ - the technique used in RyotaK's claude-code-action prompt-injection chain to steal ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN credentials from the workflow env.
references:
  - https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/claude-code-github-action-flaw-let-one.html
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/cat'
      - '/head'
      - '/xxd'
      - '/od'
      - '/strings'
      - '/tr'
      - '/awk'
      - '/grep'
      - '/sed'
      - '/tail'
      - '/dd'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
  selection_target:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/proc/'
      - '/environ'
  selection_runner_ctx:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'Runner.Worker'
      - '_work/_actions'
      - '_work/_temp'
      - 'claude-code-action'
      - 'anthropics/claude-code'
  condition: selection_image and selection_target and selection_runner_ctx
falsepositives:
  - Developer or SRE manually debugging a workflow env
  - Process-introspection tooling (osquery, psutil-based monitoring) that legitimately inspects /proc
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*"/proc/self/environ"* OR *"/environ"*)) (@process.executable.path:(*/cat OR */head OR */xxd OR */od OR */strings OR */tr OR */awk OR */grep OR */sed OR */tail OR */bash OR */sh OR */python OR */python3 OR */node) OR @process.name:(cat OR head OR xxd OR od OR strings OR bash OR sh OR python OR python3 OR node)) (@process.parent_process.command_line:(*"Runner.Worker"* OR *"_work/_actions"* OR *"claude-code-action"* OR *"anthropics/claude-code"*) OR @process.executable.path:*"/actions-runner/"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| event_platform=Lin
| CommandLine=/\/proc\/(self|[0-9]+)\/environ/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(cat|head|xxd|od|strings|tr|awk|grep|sed|tail|dd|bash|sh|python3?|node)$/i
| ParentCommandLine=/(Runner\.Worker|_work\/_actions|_work\/_temp|claude-code-action|anthropics\/claude-code|actions-runner)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count(as=executions))

Self-hosted Actions runner egress to non-allowlisted host during claude-code-action execution AICommand & Control Medium
Catches the exfiltration leg of the chain: prompt-injected Claude making outbound HTTP(S) from the runner to attacker infrastructure (article notes Claude can be coaxed to embed stolen secrets in URL path args via `gh`, `curl`, `wget` or node `fetch`). Allowlists the only destinations a legitimate claude-code-action job should hit (GitHub APIs, Anthropic, github-hosted release/object stores, GitHub App auth) — anything else from a Claude-Code-context process is a candidate for token exfil. Rationale: Allowlist is derived directly from the action's documented integrations (GitHub APIs for repo ops, Anthropic for the LLM, package mirrors for setup-* actions). The v1.0.94 fix that 'blocks exfiltration-capable URL patterns' confirms outbound URL-arg abuse was the real exfil channel, so any unexpected destination from a runner-context node/python/curl/wget/gh process is the signal. Cross-checked against the GMO Flatt Security writeup (specifically the gh-CLI weaponisation section) and the v1.0.94 security.md. Cross-checked against: • https://flatt.tech/research/posts/poisoning-claude-code-one-github-issue-to-break-the-supply-chain/ • https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/main/docs/security.md • https://cyberpress.org/claude-code-github-actions-flaw/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Workflow step legitimately calling a third-party API (Slack webhook, Datadog ingest, Sentry, Codecov) — these will fire and need allowlisting per-repo
  • npm/yarn/pnpm registry mirrors not on the allowlist (e.g. private Verdaccio, Artifactory, Nexus) — common in enterprise
  • setup-node / setup-python downloading the toolchain tarball from non-standard mirror
  • Custom actions doing HTTP scraping or webhook delivery as part of the build (e.g. release notification)
  • CDN-hosted dependency resolution (cloudflare-hosted package indexes)
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("slack.com","sentry.io","datadoghq.com","codecov.io","sonarcloud.io","artifactory","nexus","verdaccio","cloudfront.net")) and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup-node") and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup-python")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pivot from the network connection back to the runner's workflow run — pull `/home/runner/_diag/Worker_*.log` for the corresponding job and inspect the issue/PR body the action triaged. Check whether the destination resolves to a known IP-reputation hit or a freshly registered domain (DomainTools / VirusTotal). If the egress is HTTPS to a destination where the URL path encodes long base64-ish strings, treat as high-confidence exfil. 2) CONTAIN: kill the runner job, isolate the runner host, revoke the GitHub App installation token used by that run (Anthropic side) and rotate any secret the workflow had access to (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, deployment keys, npm publish tokens). Block the destination FQDN/IP at egress proxy. 3) HUNT: search prior 30 days for the same parent-process → destination pair to find pre-disclosure exploitation; correlate with GitHub audit log `workflow_run.created` events on the same repo where the actor login ends in `[bot]` to identify the initial-access pa

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
