Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TA4922 Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader / SilentRunLoader Known SHA256 Execution · [LLM] RomulusLoader: AnyDesk or SyncFuture written/spawned from non-installer parent · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TA4922 Known C2 IPs and Domains (Proofpoint Jun-2026) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SilentRunLoader: Python process touching Chrome Login Data / Cookies / Local State · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
TA4922 Known C2 IPs and Domains (Proofpoint Jun-2026) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host- and network-layer touches of the six TA4922 C2 IPs and three domains tied to Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader / SilentRunLoader staging from the Proofpoint write-up. Article-specific because the IOC set is unique to this campaign cluster. Rationale: Six C2 IPs + three domains are explicitly enumerated in the Proofpoint-derived IOC bundle and are unique to the TA4922 cluster. Direct IOC match — no behavioural heuristic needed.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-research VM detonations of the same samples
  • Internal honeypot/decoy traffic deliberately resolving the IOCs
  • SOC analyst manual lookups (whois/curl) of indicators
  • TI-feed validation tooling sending probes to confirm liveness
  • Mis-typed legitimate domain that happens to match a wildcard
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","honeypot","ti-research"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pivot on the DeviceName / SourceUserName — confirm whether the host had a recent email click or sample download tied to HR/tax/invoice lures (TA4922 themes). Pull the initiating process for the first connection. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host via Defender / EDR network-isolation; force credential reset for the logged-on user (Chrome cookies/passwords likely exfiltrated if SilentRunLoader ran). 3) HUNT: sweep the entire estate for the same IOC set across the prior 30 days, check email gateway for HR/tax/invoice lures from the same sender domains, and pivot on the SHA256 hashes in the companion UC.

let ta4922_domains = dynamic(["ws.ztts88.cyou","aeya388.club","nwphotoblog.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

TA4922 Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader / SilentRunLoader Known SHA256 Execution AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or file-drop of the eight TA4922 payload hashes Proofpoint disclosed. Article-specific because the hash set ties directly to the Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader / SilentRunLoader builds used in the March-April 2026 UK/Germany/Italy/SA campaigns. Rationale: Eight SHA256s are explicitly tied to Atlas RAT, RomulusLoader and SilentRunLoader payloads in the article-supplied IOC bundle. Hash match is the highest-fidelity pivot available.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-detonation lab VMs running the IOC sample for analysis
  • SOC reverse-engineering host with sample on disk
  • Anti-virus signature update referencing the hash in a definition file (rare but seen with ESET / Defender pattern files)
  • TI ingestion tooling caching sample bytes on disk
  • Backup snapshots of an old infected host being restored
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malwarelab","reverse"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the matching SHA256 and identify which family (Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader / SilentRunLoader) by file path + parent process; pull the email/URL that delivered it. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the device, kill the matching process tree, block the SHA256 in EDR custom indicators, and queue a forced credential rotation for the user (especially Chrome-stored credentials if SilentRunLoader). 3) HUNT: pivot from the device to the user's mailbox for the originating HR/tax/invoice lure, query email gateway for the same sender/subject across the org, and run the companion C2 IOC UC over the same time window.

SilentRunLoader: Python process touching Chrome Login Data / Cookies / Local State AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the SilentRunLoader pattern from the article — a Python-based loader (or its dropped EXE) reading Chrome credential / cookie / DPAPI master-key files. Article explicitly calls out Chrome credential, cookie and browsing-history harvest by a 'vibe-coded Python loader' delivered via UK tax-themed lures. Rationale: Article explicitly calls out a Python-based SilentRunLoader dropping an EXE to harvest Chrome credentials, cookies and browsing data. Pivot on python.exe + Chrome credential-vault paths is precisely the documented behaviour.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer Selenium / Playwright Python tests reading Chrome profile during CI
  • Password-manager bulk-import tooling (e.g. 1Password / Bitwarden CLI written in Python)
  • Forensic IR toolkits packaged as Python EXEs (chromepass, sharpchromium)
  • Browser-profile sync / migration scripts run during fleet refresh
  • Internal red-team tooling staged in AppData\Roaming
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("selenium","playwright","chromedriver","pyChromeDevTools")) and not(DeviceName has_any ("ci-","build-","redteam"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the parent of python.exe — confirm whether it traces to an email attachment / archive opened from the UK tax / HR / benefits lure mentioned in the article. Pull the python command line and any --c2 / --upload flags. 2) CONTAIN: kill the python process tree, isolate the host, expire and rotate all credentials Chrome had stored for the user (treat as compromised), invalidate active session cookies in IdP. 3) HUNT: search EmailEvents for the original lure sender; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound POSTs from the same python PID; sweep the org for the same Chrome-file-by-python pattern over 30d.
let ChromeArtifacts = dynamic([
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Cookies",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Network\Cookies",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\History",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Web Data",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Local State"
]);
let StagingPaths = dynamic([@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (ChromeArtifacts) or FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Local State","Web Data")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (StagingPaths)
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let ChromeArtifacts = dynamic([
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Cookies",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Network\Cookies",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\History",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Web Data",
  @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Local State"
]);
let StagingPaths = dynamic([@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\"]);
let PythonBins = dynamic(["python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe"]);
let BrowserBins = dynamic(["chrome.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (ChromeArtifacts) or TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Local State","Web Data")
| extend ActingBin = tolower(ActingProcessName)
| where (ActingBin in (PythonBins))
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (StagingPaths))
| where not (ActingBin in (BrowserBins))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RomulusLoader: AnyDesk or SyncFuture written/spawned from non-installer parent AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the RomulusLoader hand-off from the Mid-April 2026 campaign — the loader deploys AnyDesk and SyncFuture via DLL side-loading rather than the vendor installer. Article-specific: legitimate AnyDesk/SyncFuture installs come from msiexec / vendor setup; spawning from a script-host, archive extractor or temp-path parent is the documented TA4922 pattern. Rationale: Article states the Mid-April 2026 campaign uses RomulusLoader to deploy AnyDesk and SyncFuture via DLL side-loading. Legitimate installs originate from msiexec / vendor setup binary in Program Files; everything else against these two specific binaries is high-signal because SyncFuture is uncommon enterprise software.
ATT&CKT1219 T1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT manually launching AnyDesk portable build for ad-hoc remote support
  • SCCM / Intune custom wrapper deploying AnyDesk MSI via a non-standard parent
  • User running the AnyDesk portable executable from Downloads after a manual download
  • Approved RMM rollout where AnyDesk is wrapped inside a vendor agent binary not on the allow-list
  • Self-extracting installer (7z SFX) extracting and launching AnyDesk during a sanctioned deploy
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("sccm.exe","ccmexec.exe","intunewinapputil.exe","sysmgmt")) and not (DeviceName has_any ("itadmin","helpdesk"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the parent process tree all the way to user-mode entrypoint — confirm whether the parent is a script host (wscript / cscript / python), an archive extractor (7z / WinRAR / Explorer extracting a ZIP), or an unsigned binary in a staging path. Validate against IT's RMM-deployment runbook. 2) CONTAIN: kill AnyDesk/SyncFuture and the parent process; isolate the host; block AnyDesk inbound on perimeter; capture AnyDesk client logs (%APPDATA%\AnyDesk\connection_trace.txt) to identify operator IDs. 3) HUNT: pivot on the same SHA256 across the org, query DeviceNetworkEvents for boot.net.anydesk.com and TA4922 C2 IPs from the companion UC, search RegistryEvents for AnyDesk service install and verify whether unattended-access password was set (HKLM\SOFTWARE\AnyDesk).
let LegitInstallers = dynamic(["msiexec.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe","explorer.exe","services.exe","wusa.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","anydesk-setup.exe","anydeskmsi.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","SyncFuture.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (LegitInstallers)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LegitInstallers = dynamic(["msiexec.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe","explorer.exe","services.exe","wusa.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","anydesk-setup.exe","anydeskmsi.exe"]);
let TargetChildren = dynamic(["anydesk.exe","syncfuture.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ChildBin = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| extend ParentBin = tolower(tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ChildBin in (TargetChildren)
| where not (ParentBin in (LegitInstallers))
| where not (ParentProcessName startswith @"C:\Program Files")
| where not (ParentProcessName startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AnyDesk or SyncFuture Spawned from Non-Installer Parent
id: ace5d6f7-4567-4a9a-bcde-f01234567890
description: Detects AnyDesk.exe or SyncFuture.exe being launched by a parent process that is NOT a legitimate installer / Windows service / Program Files binary. Maps to TA4922 RomulusLoader RMM-deployment pattern from Proofpoint June 2026.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-ta4922-expands-phishing.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1574.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\AnyDesk.exe'
      - '\SyncFuture.exe'
  filter_installer_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\msiexec.exe'
      - '\setup.exe'
      - '\installer.exe'
      - '\explorer.exe'
      - '\services.exe'
      - '\wusa.exe'
      - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'

      - 'C:\Program Files (x86)\'

  - SCCM / Intune managed-app deployment via non-standard agent
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @Image:(*\AnyDesk.exe OR *\anydesk.exe OR *\ANYDESK.EXE OR *\SyncFuture.exe OR *\syncfuture.exe OR *\SYNCFUTURE.EXE) -@ParentImage:(*\msiexec.exe OR *\MSIEXEC.EXE OR *\setup.exe OR *\Setup.exe OR *\installer.exe OR *\Installer.exe OR *\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.exe OR *\EXPLORER.EXE OR *\services.exe OR *\Services.exe OR *\wusa.exe OR *\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\AnyDesk-Setup.exe OR *\AnyDeskMSI.exe OR *"\Program Files\"* OR *"\Program Files (x86)\"*)

| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/^(msiexec|setup|installer|explorer|services|wusa|TrustedInstaller|AnyDesk[-_]?Setup|AnyDeskMSI)\.exe$/i
| NOT ParentImageFileName=/\\Program Files( \(x86\))?\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |

    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.

CloudAppEvents

AuditLogs

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

SecurityEvent

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hypotheses, telemetry, and human judgment: Inside Cisco Talos Threat Hunting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest dropping script.ps1 to user AppData (KongTuke stage-2)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] KongTuke TDS C2 callout to 144.31.221.82:6060 with /capcha URL path · [LLM] Same host calling KongTuke C2 from both powershell.exe and curl.exe within short window · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
KongTuke TDS C2 callout to 144.31.221.82:6060 with /capcha URL path AICommand & Control High
Hunts the specific KongTuke (TAG-124 / 404 TDS) command-and-control infrastructure named in the Talos case study: outbound HTTP to 144.31.221.82 on TCP/6060 with a URL path matching the KongTuke /capcha* fingerprint. Single-IOC alerting because all three values are article-named. Rationale: Single high-confidence IOC bundle straight from the Talos case-study paragraph: IP 144.31.221.82, TCP/6060, URL path /capcha9856. The /capcha* fingerprint is corroborated by Recorded Future (TAG-124), Red Canary KongTuke profile, and malware-traffic-analysis.net Jan 2026 KongTuke ClickFix capture. Cross-checked via WebSearch — KongTuke is a real, active TDS. Cross-checked against: • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/kongtuke/ • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-124-multi-layered-tds-infrastructure-extensive-user-base • https://www.malware-traffic-analysis.net/2026/01/08/index.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest or red-team rehearsal targeting the same IOC after reading the Talos blog
  • Threat-intel platform or DFIR sandbox automatically dialling out to known-bad C2 for verification (e.g. JoeSandbox, ANY.RUN agent on a corp jump host)
  • Threat-hunt tooling that replays packet captures with the destination IP rewritten for test purposes
  • Security awareness training simulator using captured KongTuke traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("smss.exe","wininit.exe") and not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","sbox","detonation","malsandbox"))
Response runbook
Triage: Confirm the source host is a real production endpoint, then pull DeviceProcessEvents on it for ±30 min around the connection. Look for cmd.exe → powershell.exe -EncodedCommand → curl.exe chain that Talos documented. Check Defender/AMP for any blocked-detection signatures on the same host. Contain: Isolate the host via Defender for Endpoint / Falcon Network Containment. Block 144.31.221.82 + the /capcha URL pattern at the firewall and proxy. Force-reset the logged-in user's credentials. Hunt: Sweep the entire estate for any other endpoint connecting to 144.31.221.82, port 6060, or any URL containing /capcha. Check WordPress/CMS site referrer logs for which compromised site redirected the user (TDS chains). Submit the IP to TI vendors and enrol the URL-path pattern into the proxy as a hunt rule.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "144.31.221.82"
   or (RemotePort == 6060 and RemoteUrl has "/capcha")
   or RemoteUrl has "/capcha9856"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessParentFileName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Cisco" or DeviceProduct has "Firepower" or DeviceProduct has "Secure Firewall" or isnotempty(DestinationIP)
| where DestinationIP == "144.31.221.82"
   or (DestinationPort == 6060 and RequestURL has "/capcha")
   or RequestURL has "/capcha9856"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: KongTuke TDS C2 to 144.31.221.82 / capcha URL Path
id: 7e3b1f4e-1f0e-4a2e-9b8d-6b1f4e3c2a01
description: Detects outbound network traffic to KongTuke TDS C2 infrastructure (144.31.221.82:6060) or any URL path matching the KongTuke /capcha* fingerprint reported by Cisco Talos.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/hypotheses-telemetry-and-human-judgment-inside-cisco-talos-threat-hunting/
  - https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-124-multi-layered-tds-infrastructure-extensive-user-base
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp: '144.31.221.82'
  selection_port_path:
    DestinationPort: 6060
    DestinationHostname|contains: '/capcha'
  selection_path:
    Url|contains: '/capcha9856'
  condition: selection_ip or selection_port_path or selection_path
falsepositives:

PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest dropping script.ps1 to user AppData (KongTuke stage-2) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the KongTuke stage-2 download pattern from the Talos case study: a powershell.exe process whose command line invokes Invoke-WebRequest (or iwr) and writes a file named script.ps1 into the user's ApplicationData / AppData directory. Pairs the URL-fetch verb, the article-named filename, and the article-named drop location in one event. Rationale: The combination of three article-named tokens in one PowerShell command line — Invoke-WebRequest verb, exact filename script.ps1, and AppData/ApplicationData drop path — collapses to one cmdline-substring detection that's high specificity. Sourced directly from the Talos KongTuke walk-through (cmd.exe → powershell.exe -EncodedCommand → IWR → script.ps1 → ApplicationData). Cross-checked against: • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/kongtuke/ • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-124-multi-layered-tds-infrastructure-extensive-user-base
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin debugging an internal PowerShell module by manually fetching a generic 'script.ps1' into AppData
  • Software install wrapper that downloads a setup script (rename script.ps1 → install.ps1 is more common, but some installers do this)
  • Red-team / atomic-red-team test cases that mirror the KongTuke download chain
  • Security researcher rehydrating IOCs in a lab VM joined to corporate Defender
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("vscode.exe","code.exe","devenv.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe") and not (DeviceName has_any ("sbx","sandbox","redteam","atomic"))
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the parent process tree for the powershell.exe event — confirm parent is cmd.exe spawned from a browser process (chrome/edge/firefox), which matches the TDS-redirect chain. Decode any preceding -EncodedCommand on the same PID. Hash and submit the dropped script.ps1 (still in %AppData%) to sandbox; capture content before Remove-Item runs. Contain: Isolate the host. Suspend the affected user account. Block C2 144.31.221.82 + /capcha pattern at egress. Hunt: Sweep estate for any powershell.exe with script.ps1 + AppData in cmdline. Pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for that PID/host and confirm C2 callback. Pull browser history for the user to find the compromised WordPress redirector that launched the TDS chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "Net.WebClient", "DownloadFile", "DownloadString")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "script.ps1"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData", "ApplicationData", "\\Roaming\\", "\\Local\\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "Net.WebClient", "DownloadFile", "DownloadString")
| where CommandLine has "script.ps1"
| where CommandLine has_any ("AppData", "ApplicationData", "\\Roaming\\", "\\Local\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: KongTuke PowerShell Drops script.ps1 to AppData via Invoke-WebRequest
id: 7e3b1f4e-1f0e-4a2e-9b8d-6b1f4e3c2a02
description: Detects PowerShell command line that fetches a remote file named script.ps1 and writes it into the user's AppData directory — the KongTuke stage-2 download chain documented by Cisco Talos.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/hypotheses-telemetry-and-human-judgment-inside-cisco-talos-threat-hunting/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_fetch:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'iwr '
      - 'Net.WebClient'
      - 'DownloadFile'
      - 'DownloadString'
  selection_file:
    CommandLine|contains: 'script.ps1'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'AppData'
      - 'ApplicationData'
      - '\Roaming\'
      - '\Local\'
  condition: all of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate internal scripts that happen to fetch a file named script.ps1 into AppData (rare; review user context)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe)) AND (@CommandLine:(*Invoke-WebRequest* OR *iwr\ * OR *Net.WebClient* OR *DownloadFile* OR *DownloadString*)) AND @CommandLine:*script.ps1* AND (@CommandLine:(*AppData* OR *ApplicationData* OR *\\Roaming\\* OR *\\Local\\*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(Invoke-WebRequest|iwr |Net\.WebClient|DownloadFile|DownloadString)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("script\.ps1", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(AppData|ApplicationData|\\\\Roaming\\\\|\\\\Local\\\\)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdlines values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parents from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*iwr *" OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*") Processes.process="*script.ps1*" (Processes.process="*AppData*" OR Processes.process="*ApplicationData*" OR Processes.process="*\\Roaming\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Local\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Same host calling KongTuke C2 from both powershell.exe and curl.exe within short window AICommand & Control High
Reproduces the Talos multi-source-correlation insight: the same endpoint reaching 144.31.221.82 from two distinct binaries (powershell.exe via Invoke-WebRequest and curl.exe directly) is the disambiguating signal that turned a single firewall hit into a confirmed intrusion. Single-binary callouts to the IP are already caught by UC1; this UC fires on the host-level fan-out only. Rationale: Directly encodes the Talos case-study insight: 'a separate curl.exe process making requests to the same C2 infrastructure the firewall had flagged.' Two distinct LOLBin/native binaries calling the same KongTuke IP from one host is high-fidelity even without the URL-path filter — it's the multi-process fan-out that confirms intrusion vs single-shot scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://redcanary.com/threat-detection-report/threats/kongtuke/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT troubleshooting a connectivity issue, running both Test-NetConnection (PowerShell) and curl against the same external host
  • Monitoring agents (e.g. uptime checks) that issue parallel HTTP probes from multiple wrappers
  • Red-team simulation reproducing the Talos case study against the same IOCs
  • Custom CMDB sync script that uses both powershell IWR and curl for redundancy
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ops-","jumpbox-","netops-")) and not (AccountName has_any ("netops","sre","itadmin"))
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the process trees for both the powershell.exe and curl.exe events — confirm common parent or temporal proximity (<10 min). Decode any -EncodedCommand on the powershell side; capture curl.exe full command-line (URL, headers, output path). Verify the destination IP/path against KongTuke IOC list. Contain: Isolate the host. Force a credential reset for the logged-in user. Block 144.31.221.82 + /capcha pattern at proxy and firewall. Snapshot the host for memory analysis before reimage. Hunt: Run UC1 + UC2 across the estate to find any other host hitting KongTuke. Pivot on the IP via VirusTotal / Shodan for sibling infrastructure; add ASN to network-egress hunt block. Check email gateway for any KongTuke-themed lure URL that arrived in the 24h before first observation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "144.31.221.82" or (RemotePort == 6060 and RemoteUrl has "/capcha")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe")
| summarize ProcessSet = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            FirstConnection = min(Timestamp),
            LastConnection = max(Timestamp),
            ConnectionCount = count(),
            CmdLines = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 8)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteIP, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where array_length(ProcessSet) >= 2
| where (ProcessSet has "curl.exe") and (ProcessSet has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe"))
| order by FirstConnection desc
let WindowHours = 1h;
let FirewallHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DestinationIP == "144.31.221.82" or (DestinationPort == 6060 and RequestURL has "/capcha")
    | project FirewallTime=TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL;
let ProcessHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
         or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
         or NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
    | where CommandLine has_any ("144.31.221.82", "capcha", "script.ps1")
         or NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
    | project ProcessTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, NewProcessName, CommandLine, SubjectUserName;
FirewallHits
| join kind=inner (
    ProcessHits
    | summarize Procs=make_set(NewProcessName), AnyCmd=make_set(CommandLine, 8) by Computer
    | where array_length(Procs) >= 2
) on $left.SourceIP == $right.Computer
| order by FirewallTime desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:144.31.221.82 @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\Curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="144.31.221.82"
| ContextImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|curl)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[collect([ContextImageFileName]), count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
| length(ContextImageFileName) >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_procs values(Processes.process_name) as procs values(Processes.process) as cmdlines min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe") (Processes.process="*144.31.221.82*" OR Processes.process="*capcha*") by Processes.dest Processes.user host
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| where distinct_procs >= 2
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Processes.process_name) as distinct_procs values(Processes.process_name) as procs values(Processes.process) as cmdlines min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe") (Processes.process="*144.31.221.82*" OR Processes.process="*capcha*") by Processes.dest Processes.user host

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

FlutterShell Backdoor Spreads to macOS via Malicious Google and YouTube Ads

The Hacker News
2026-06-04 12 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a macOS malvertising campaign codenamed Operation FlutterBridge that spreads a new backdoor called FlutterShell. According to Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, the campaign is said to be the next stage of a previously reported activity cluster dubbed JSCoreRunner (aka FileRipple) in late August 2025. The cybercrime group behind the two attack chains is

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Chrome Preferences tamper on macOS by non-Chrome process (FlutterShell browser hijack) · [LLM] Known FlutterShell SHA256 binary execution on macOS · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] macOS host beaconing to FlutterShell C2 / ad-intermediary domains · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] FlutterShell WebView bridge spawns shell on macOS (arbitrary command execution capability) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Chrome Preferences tamper on macOS by non-Chrome process (FlutterShell browser hijack) AIInstallation High
FlutterShell rewrites Google Chrome configuration files on macOS to force traffic through an attacker-controlled ad-intermediary site. This hunts writes to Chrome's Preferences/Local State by any process other than Chrome itself, which is the article-specific browser-hijack tell. Rationale: Anchors on the article's most specific operational behaviour: "modifies Google Chrome configuration files to hijack the browser, forcing all traffic through an attacker-controlled, ad-filled intermediary site." Filtering for non-Chrome writers eliminates almost all baseline Chrome self-writes. Cross-checked against Unit 42 / Palo Alto Networks blog coverage of JSCoreRunner/FileRipple. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
ATT&CKT1176 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome MDM/configuration management tools writing managed policy files
  • Chrome enterprise extensions installer rewriting Preferences on first launch
  • Keystone (Chrome's updater) writing state during version upgrades
  • Backup utilities (Time Machine, Carbon Copy Cloner) touching Preferences files during restore
  • Third-party password managers (1Password, Bitwarden) syncing browser session data
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("GoogleSoftwareUpdateAgent","GoogleSoftwareUpdateDaemon","ksadmin","ksinstall"))
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/Library/Google/GoogleSoftwareUpdate/")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName + SHA256 writing the Chrome config. Hash-check against VirusTotal and Apple notarization records — FlutterShell binaries were notarized so notarization alone is NOT exoneration. Pull a 24h process tree to identify how the binary was delivered (Downloads folder, dmg mount, malvertising click). 2. Contain: Isolate the macOS host. Revoke Chrome browser sessions for the user (force re-auth on all SSO apps). Reset Chrome by removing the affected Preferences/Local State files. Push the binary hash + signer cert to MDE block list. 3. Hunt: Pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet. Hunt DNS to atsheisdomestic.org, etoftheappyrince.org, healightejustb.org, sinterfumesco.com, ads-parkpro.com, adsparkpro.top, adsparkpro.net, softwe.art. Check for sibling variants named PodcastsLounge, PDF-Brain, PDF-Ninja on other hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/"
| where FileName in~ ("Preferences","Secure Preferences","Local State")
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Google Chrome","Google Chrome Helper","chrome","Keystone"))
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Preferences","Secure Preferences","Local State")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("Google Chrome","chrome","Keystone"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
title: Non-Chrome Process Modifies Chrome Preferences on macOS
id: 9e2a3f51-5b8a-4f6d-9c2a-7d4b1c0e5a11
description: Detects modification of Google Chrome Preferences / Local State files on macOS by any process other than Chrome itself, indicative of FlutterShell-style browser-hijack adware redirecting traffic through an attacker-controlled intermediary.
references:

  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/
author: SOC Detection Eng

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: macos
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Preferences'
      - '/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Secure Preferences'
      - '/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Local State'
  filter_chrome:
    Image|contains:
      - '/Google Chrome.app/'
      - '/Keystone.app/'

level: high
source:(macos.osquery OR macos.endpoint) @file.path:(*"/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Preferences"* OR *"/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default/Secure Preferences"* OR *"/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Local State"*) -@process.executable.path:(*"/Google Chrome.app/"* OR *"/Keystone.app/"*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/\/Library\/Application Support\/Google\/Chrome\/Default\/Preferences$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/Library\/Application Support\/Google\/Chrome\/Default\/Secure Preferences$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/Library\/Application Support\/Google\/Chrome\/Local State$/i)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/Google Chrome/
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/Keystone/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

macOS host beaconing to FlutterShell C2 / ad-intermediary domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution or network connections from macOS endpoints to the article's named FlutterShell infrastructure (ads-parkpro/adsparkpro/softwe.art front-company domains plus the four C2 cover domains). High-fidelity given the IOCs come straight from Unit 42's IOC list and are unlikely to appear in any legitimate macOS workload. Rationale: Direct match on Unit 42's named infrastructure for Operation FlutterBridge. Domains correspond to article-stated front companies (AdsParkPro LTD, SOFT WE ART LIMITED) and C2 cover. Domains have no legitimate use in any enterprise; one hit warrants an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst manually browsing IOCs from a research VM
  • Sandbox / detonation environments deliberately resolving IOCs
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion pipelines doing DNS lookups for enrichment
  • DNS sinkhole / blackhole resolver responses being logged twice
  • Web proxy / SSL inspection appliance test traffic
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonate","malware-lab","researcher"))
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3")) // suppress likely manual IOC lookups
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull initiating process + parent process from DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsRequest. Validate the device is a production endpoint not a research/sandbox VM. Pull file hash of initiating process and check VirusTotal — match against article SHA256s. 2. Contain: Isolate device via MDE. Sinkhole the 8 domains at egress DNS. Force user password + session reset (Chrome cookies likely stolen per article's "browser session data theft" capability). 3. Hunt: Pivot on the initiating SHA256 across the fleet. Hunt for Apple-signed binaries with Developer ID matching AdsParkPro LTD, Advantage Web Marketing LLC, or SOFT WE ART LIMITED / PACIFIC TRADE SOLUTIONS LTD signers. Hunt for sibling FlutterShell variant names PodcastsLounge, PDF-Brain, PDF-Ninja in DeviceFileEvents.
let c2_domains = dynamic(["atsheisdomestic.org","etoftheappyrince.org","healightejustb.org","sinterfumesco.com","ads-parkpro.com","adsparkpro.top","adsparkpro.net","softwe.art"]);
let net = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let dns = DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| extend QName = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).QueryName)
| where QName has_any (c2_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, QName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
union net, dns
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2_domains = dynamic(["atsheisdomestic.org","etoftheappyrince.org","healightejustb.org","sinterfumesco.com","ads-parkpro.com","adsparkpro.top","adsparkpro.net","softwe.art"]);
let dns_hits = ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (c2_domains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct;
let net_hits = ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any (c2_domains) or DstHostname has_any (c2_domains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, DstIpAddr, EventProduct;
union dns_hits, net_hits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known FlutterShell SHA256 binary execution on macOS AIInstallation Medium
Direct hash-match alert on the eight FlutterShell SHA256s published by Unit 42 for the PodcastsLounge / PDF-Brain / PDF-Ninja variants. Defender XDR + Sentinel + Falcon all surface SHA256 on process telemetry — minimum-friction high-fidelity tripwire for in-the-wild samples. Rationale: Unit 42 IOC SHA256s are tier-1 confidence and shared across three FlutterShell variants. Notarized signing means file-reputation alone won't catch these; hash-match is the cleanest tripwire. Cross-referenced against Unit 42 IOC bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://www.virustotal.com/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1553.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst downloading the sample to a sandbox VM for analysis
  • Sample uploaded to an internal malware repository for triage
  • File-integrity monitoring rescanning a quarantined sample after policy update
  • SOAR/EDR scheduled VT-enrichment job reading the file from quarantine
  • DFIR replaying a captured artifact in a forensics lab
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonate","malware-lab","forensics","-fir-"))
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/Quarantine/","/SampleVault/","/MalwareSamples/"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm the device is a production endpoint not a sandbox/research host. Pull the Apple Developer ID signer of the binary — if it matches AdsParkPro / Advantage Web Marketing / SOFT WE ART / PACIFIC TRADE SOLUTIONS, escalate immediately and report cert for revocation to Apple. 2. Contain: Isolate the host. Add binary hash + signer cert to MDE block list. Force user re-auth across all SSO apps (FlutterShell steals browser session data). 3. Hunt: Sweep entire fleet for the 8 hashes (90-day lookback). Pull DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl on the dropped binary to identify the malvertising landing page. Pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountName to find other affected users.

| where Timestamp > ago(90d)

FlutterShell WebView bridge spawns shell on macOS (arbitrary command execution capability) AIActions on Objectives Medium
FlutterShell uses a JavaScript-to-native bridge inside a WebView to invoke shell commands on demand from attacker-controlled JavaScript. Hunts macOS Flutter-style apps (signed with the article's known shell-company developers, or matching the named variant binary names) spawning /bin/sh, /bin/bash, /usr/bin/zsh, /usr/bin/osascript — the smoking-gun behaviour of the JS-bridge backdoor. Rationale: Anchors on the article's three named variant binaries (PodcastsLounge, PDF-Brain, PDF-Ninja) AND the WebView-JS-bridge architecture that necessitates spawning a shell to execute attacker-supplied commands. A legitimate PDF reader or podcast app has no reason to fork /bin/sh. The signer-name pivot (AdsParkPro / Advantage Web Marketing / SOFT WE ART / PACIFIC TRADE SOLUTIONS) catches future variants that change the binary name. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Flutter desktop apps using platform channels for non-malicious purposes (rare on macOS productivity software)
  • Electron-based PDF readers invoking helper scripts during install
  • Developer-built proof-of-concept macOS apps with the same names in test environments
  • macOS app uninstaller scripts running during user-initiated removal
  • System Preferences automation via osascript during legitimate user workflow
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--version","--help","-V"))
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/Applications/Xcode.app/")
| where not(AccountName has "developer" and DeviceName has_any ("dev-","-dev","build-"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Capture the full child cmdline — look for `do shell script`, `printenv`, `env`, base64 strings, or remote URLs (curl|wget) which confirm backdoor exec vs benign helper. Hash-check the parent app against Unit 42 IOCs. 2. Contain: Isolate the host. Kill the parent process tree. Quarantine the .app bundle and pull the embedded Info.plist signer + bundle ID for revocation reporting to Apple. Reset user credentials and Chrome sessions. 3. Hunt: Pivot on InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName across the fleet for all binaries signed by the four named shell companies. Hunt DeviceNetworkEvents for the JS-bridge fetching new logic from the C2 domains (UC 2). Look for environment-variable exfiltration in process command lines (`env`, `printenv`, `launchctl getenv`).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("PodcastsLounge","PDF-Brain","PDF-Ninja")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/PodcastsLounge.app/","/PDF-Brain.app/","/PDF-Ninja.app/")
   or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("AdsParkPro","Advantage Web Marketing","SOFT WE ART","PACIFIC TRADE SOLUTIONS")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","zsh","dash","osascript","curl","python","python3","env")
| extend HasShellArgs = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","-c\"","-e ","do shell script","printenv","env")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HasShellArgs
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("PodcastsLounge","PDF-Brain","PDF-Ninja")
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("/PodcastsLounge.app/","/PDF-Brain.app/","/PDF-Ninja.app/")
   or ActingProcessFileCompany has_any ("AdsParkPro","Advantage Web Marketing","SOFT WE ART","PACIFIC TRADE SOLUTIONS")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bin/sh","/bin/bash","/bin/zsh","/bin/dash","/usr/bin/osascript","/usr/bin/curl","/usr/bin/python","/usr/bin/python3","/usr/bin/env")
| extend HasShellArgs = TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","do shell script","printenv","env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessFileCompany, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, HasShellArgs, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FlutterShell macOS App Spawns Unix Shell or AppleScript
id: c1f4e802-7b6d-4a13-9c5e-3f8a0d2b4e76
description: Detects FlutterShell-variant macOS apps (PodcastsLounge / PDF-Brain / PDF-Ninja) or binaries signed by article-named shell-company developers spawning /bin/sh, /bin/bash, /bin/zsh, /usr/bin/osascript or curl/python — indicative of the JS-to-native bridge executing attacker commands.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fluttershell-backdoor-spreads-to-macos.html
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.002
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: macos
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - '/PodcastsLounge.app/'
      - '/PDF-Brain.app/'
      - '/PDF-Ninja.app/'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bin/sh'
      - '/bin/bash'
      - '/bin/zsh'
      - '/bin/dash'
      - '/usr/bin/osascript'
      - '/usr/bin/curl'
      - '/usr/bin/python'
      - '/usr/bin/python3'
      - '/usr/bin/env'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: high
source:(macos.osquery OR macos.endpoint OR macos.unifiedlog) (@process.parent.executable.path:(*"/PodcastsLounge.app/"* OR *"/PDF-Brain.app/"* OR *"/PDF-Ninja.app/"*) OR @process.parent.name:(PodcastsLounge OR PDF-Brain OR PDF-Ninja)) @process.executable.path:(*"/bin/sh" OR *"/bin/bash" OR *"/bin/zsh" OR *"/usr/bin/osascript" OR *"/usr/bin/curl" OR *"/usr/bin/python" OR *"/usr/bin/python3" OR *"/usr/bin/env")
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ParentBaseFileName=/^(PodcastsLounge|PDF-Brain|PDF-Ninja)$/i OR ParentImageFileName=/\/(PodcastsLounge|PDF-Brain|PDF-Ninja)\.app\//i)
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|zsh|dash|osascript|curl|python3?|env)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
